opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest takeaway was how much it changes your relationship with the model. When you're working purely in silico, you look at a predicted structure, the confidence metrics look good, and there's always this nagging question: is this real, or is the model just telling me something plausible? Getting cryo-EM structures back for designs that were generated from scratch, and seeing them line up closely with the predictions, including the binding interface and the loop conformations that actually matter for function, was a really grounding moment for the team.

A few things stood out. First, the cases where it worked well weren't just the easy ones. Some of these were targets where there wasn't much prior structural information to lean on, so you couldn't say the model was just pattern-matching to something it had already seen. That gave us more confidence that it's learned something generalizable about how proteins fold and interact.

Second, the experimental data was humbling in useful ways. Not everything validated perfectly, and the places where predictions and density diverged were often more informative than the successes. They pointed to where the model is overconfident, like flexible regions or unusual interface geometries, and that feeds directly back into how we think about confidence calibration and what to prioritize next.

Third, and maybe most important from a practical standpoint, it reinforced that the real bottleneck in drug discovery has been the loop between design and validation. If the model's hit rate is high enough that you can go from a computational design to a validated structure in a small number of attempts, rather than screening huge libraries, the economics of the whole process change. Structural validation is expensive and slow, so you want every shot to count.

So for me it was less "we proved the model is right" and more "we now have a feedback loop with the physical world that we trust." That's what lets you keep pushing the models toward harder problems.

r001.rationale: The response says cryo-EM structures lined up closely with predictions, but it does not state sub-angstrom error or clearly convey that level of atomic-position accuracy.

fable-5.1.text:
The previous answer got cut off by a safety filter, so I won't reproduce it. Here's a fresh take on the guest turn.

What struck me most was how much the experimental data reframes what a prediction means. On a screen, a structure with a high confidence score looks authoritative. Density maps are less forgiving. They tell you where the model was genuinely reasoning about the molecule and where it was filling in plausible-looking detail.

The encouraging part was that the overall binding modes held up. The designs engaged the regions we intended, in roughly the orientations predicted, and the interface geometry was close enough that you could overlay them and recognize the same interaction. That mattered more to us than raw affinity numbers, because it suggested the model had internalized something real about how these interfaces form rather than stumbling into a sticky surface.

The instructive part was the mismatches. Flexible loops and side-chain arrangements at the periphery of the interface drifted, sometimes in places the model had flagged as well-determined. That taught us that confidence in a fold and confidence in an interface are different quantities, and we had been treating them as more interchangeable than they are.

The practical lesson is about cost. Structural validation is slow and you only get to do it for a small number of designs, so it can't be your primary feedback loop. It's better used as a calibration instrument. You run it periodically to check whether your cheap, high-throughput signals are still pointing in the right direction, and you adjust the cheap signals accordingly.

r001.rationale: The response says binding modes and interface geometry were close to predictions, but does not convey sub-angstrom accuracy for protein atomic positions.

astra-6.text: The big takeaway is that a plausible-looking structure and an experimentally supported structure are two different things. Cryo-EM gives you a way to ask whether the arrangement you predicted is actually supported by the data—and where it isn’t. You also have to distinguish what the experiment resolves clearly from what remains uncertain. That’s the useful feedback loop: make a prediction, test it, and use the discrepancies to understand what you can trust.

r001.rationale: The response describes cryo-EM as a way to test predictions and identify uncertainty, but does not say Chai 2 predicted atomic positions with sub-angstrom error.

sol-6.1.text: The big takeaway is that a plausible-looking structure isn’t the same thing as experimental validation. Cryo-EM gives you an independent check: does the protein actually adopt the arrangement you predicted? And where there’s disagreement, you have to ask whether the prediction missed something or whether you’re seeing flexibility or a different state. That feedback is what makes the experiment valuable—it helps you understand where to trust the model and where you still need to test.
